title: The flower-sweeper's song
hookLine: Sunita, once despised, is honored by gods and people (Theragatha, Sunita)

lines: TODAY, THE NIGHT AND THE DAWN.
cards: Two crowds, one at each end of a single poem. At the start, the Buddha walks into the city with a company of monks around him, and a man who hauls away withered flowers sets down his carrying pole.

At the end, that same man sits with a company of gods around him. This is Sunita, met a few weeks ago on that street, hearing the two words that made him a monk: come, monk. Today, the night, and the dawn.

teach.b: First, the night. After the street, Sunita goes into the forest alone and does what the Teacher told him, without slacking. His song walks through the night watch by watch.
In the first watch, he says, he remembered his former lives. In the middle watch, his divine eye was made clear. In the last, he split apart the mass of darkness.

teach.h: INDRA AND BRAHMA BOW AT DAWN.
teach.b: At sunrise, Indra and Brahma come to him and bow with joined palms. The man who once bowed to everyone is now the one bowed to.

They speak: homage to you, finest of men, whose taints are destroyed; you are worthy of offerings. Offerings are what people bring, and this was a man who once lived on little to eat. Third, the mirror.

teach.h: NOW HE STANDS AMONG THE GODS.
teach.b: When the Buddha sees him, the song says, Sunita is surrounded by a company of gods, the way the Buddha was surrounded by monks on the morning they met. The poem's shape turns all the way round. Fourth, the smile.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA SMILES: A BRAHMIN BY CONDUCT.
teach.b: The Buddha smiles and speaks a verse: by discipline, by the holy life, by restraint and taming oneself, by these one becomes a brahmin; this is the highest brahmin.
In the world of the poem, brahmin names the priestly families, honored by birth. Here it names a way of living.
And Sunita doesn't gloat over the people who once looked past him. He just tells it in order: the flowers, the street, the night, the dawn.

how: Theravada teachers often tell Sunita's story, and the Buddha's closing words to him, when they teach that what makes a person noble is conduct, not birth.

o: a gift given to monks at dawn
a bow made with joined palms

s: Sunita's song walks through his night alone, watch by watch
first his former lives, then the divine eye made clear, then the darkness split apart.
the gods call Sunita worthy of offerings
homage to you, finest of men, they say; you are worthy of offerings.
Sunita's song ends with him scolding the people who despised him
it ends with the Buddha's smile and a verse: one becomes a brahmin by discipline and restraint.

games.q: you're Sunita. it's sunrise after a night alone in the forest, and Indra and Brahma stand before you with joined palms. what does the song say comes next?
o: you go back to town to show the people who mocked you.
the Buddha sees you among the gods, smiles, and speaks a verse.
you bow to the gods, as you always bowed to everyone.
games.why: the Buddha sees him surrounded by gods, as the Buddha himself was surrounded by monks the day they met, and smiles: a brahmin is made by discipline and restraint.

practice: Picture someone whose work happens before you arrive or after you leave: the person who unlocks the building, the night shift at the hospital, whoever picked the fruit in your kitchen.

See the hours they keep, the dark before dawn, and in your mind put your palms together, the way Indra and Brahma did for Sunita at sunrise. If a judgment rises, notice it, and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Dakkhineyya. Worthy of offerings: what gods called Sunita at dawn, the man who once cleared away withered flowers and was bowed to by them. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: dakkhineyya, worthy of offerings. What Indra and Brahma call Sunita at dawn.

carryVoice: Your line: once despised. By dawn, the man people looked past was called worthy of offerings. Eight hundred days now, each one counted.
